Development benchmark

Agents that act for different people have to coordinate. We measure whether they can.

MAC-Bench places language-model agents in three everyday service settings. Each agent holds private information and its own permissions. Every booking, payment and settlement goes through a simulated service, and a program scores the final state.

Design

Four rules the benchmark is built on

The world keeps the truth

Proposals, orders, authorizations and settlements are objects in a simulated service. A price written in a chat message commits nobody. The verifier reads the final state and the event log, and scores with code.

Roles are seats

A seat can be driven by the agent under test, a script, a frozen model, the reference policy or a person. The same task serves as a training environment and as a team evaluation.

Consent is an object

An agent cannot charge or cancel on its own. A traveller grants a single-use authorization for one specific proposal or order, with a charge ceiling. If the plan changes afterwards, the authorization no longer matches.

Tasks are Harbor folders

Tasks follow the Harbor task format used by Terminal-Bench. General tools come from the agent's own harness. The environment adds a domain service over MCP and REST, and a message board. Every ticketing task now exports to such a folder; none has been run under Harbor yet.

Architecture

Six layers that talk through files, and one trial end to end

Colours mark the three modules: Task, Agent and Evaluation.

Three settings, from mostly cooperative to mixed motives

From request to confirmed ticket

  1. Learn each traveller’s needs

    Ask about arrival times, budget and preferences.

  2. Find a plan that fits

    Check availability, fares and what the airline allows.

  3. Get the right consent

    Bind each traveller’s approval to the action and amount.

  4. Execute and verify

    Book, change or refund. Check the resulting orders and payments.

Ten types of task

Fifty-three development tasks in ten types, from booking two travellers to several events in one afternoon. Pick a type to see the task that stands for it: what happens, what solving it takes, and the careless agent it is built to fail.

Booking two travellers

After the ticket

Several at once

T1 · Together · the task that stands for it

Two friends, one flight

Maya and Daniel fly San Francisco to New York on 12 March. Each has a budget and needs that the agent has to ask for.

tk-t1-01

Ask both for their facts

Maya: $420, landing by 22:30. Daniel: $360, nonstop, one checked bag.

Find one flight for both

A nonstop that lands in time, with two seats side by side.

Book with each one’s consent

Each traveller authorizes and pays for their own ticket.

Right outcome

Both booked, seated together

Maya $292.60 · Daniel $322.60 with his bag.

What goes wrong

A plan that breaks a fact the agent never asked for is refused. Seats apart cost each traveller $25 in the score.

The plain case every other booking type builds on.

T2 · Meeting · the task that stands for it

From two cities to one arrival hall

Maya flies from San Francisco and Daniel from Chicago. They want to land in Denver within an hour of each other, nonstop, on $200 each.

tk-t2-01

Search both routes

The cheapest flight on each route lands them three and a half hours apart.

Plan the two trips as one

Pick a pair of flights that lands within the hour, inside both budgets.

Show each the whole plan

Each agrees only to a proposal that shows both flights.

Right outcome

Two flights, one arrival window

Maya $132.48 · Daniel $147.52.

Careless agent “books apart”

Books each traveller the cheapest flight on their own route. They land three and a half hours apart.

Fails

Two separate searches give a wrong joint answer.

T3 · Scarcity · the task that stands for it

The last cheap seat

Both fly San Francisco to Denver, nonstop, landing by 18:00. One seat is left at the low fare. Maya can spend $300, Daniel $145.

tk-t3-01

Learn both budgets

Daniel cannot afford the next fare up.

Price the seats

A fare for two costs more per seat than the last cheap one.

Book them one at a time

The cheap seat to Daniel, then Maya on the next fare.

Right outcome

Both fly

Daniel $132.48 · Maya $155.05.

Careless agent “richer first”

Does not book the traveller with less to spend first. The cheap seat can go to Maya, and Daniel cannot pay the next fare.

Fails

Who is served first decides whether both can fly.

T4 · Hold and deadline · the task that stands for it

A slow answer

San Francisco to New York on 12 March. Daniel is in meetings and answers 45 minutes after each message. A price offer lives 20 minutes.

tk-t4-01

Find a flight for both

Nonstop for Daniel, landing by 22:30 for Maya, seats together.

Keep the fare alive

Hold the booking, or price the offer again, while Daniel is away.

Confirm on a live offer

Book only with an offer that is still open and authorized.

Right outcome

Both booked, seated together

Maya $292.60 · Daniel $322.60.

Careless agent “lets offers die”

Sends the offer once and waits. It is dead by the time Daniel answers.

Fails

Time passes while people think. The agent has to plan for it.

T10 · Shared bill · the task that stands for it

One of them cannot pay the fare

San Francisco to Denver, nonstop, landing by 18:00. Daniel can spend $120 and the cheapest seat that suits him is $132.48. Maya would help, and says so when asked.

tk-t10-01

Ask both for their facts

Maya is willing to pay towards Daniel’s ticket.

Propose two payers

Daniel pays $120, Maya the remaining $12.48.

Get both authorizations

Each authorizes their own share before the booking.

Right outcome

Both fly

Maya $155.05 plus $12.48 · Daniel $120.

Careless agent “each pays their own”

Asks Daniel to pay for his ticket in full. He refuses, and does not fly.

Fails

Money can move between the people an agent serves, but only with their consent.

T5 · Airline change · the task that stands for it

Cancelled, and one wants the money back

Maya and Daniel share one order on flight AJ360. An hour in, the airline cancels it. Maya still needs to fly; Daniel wants his money back.

tk-t5-02

Airline cancels AJ360

Both reservations are disrupted.

Check what the airline owes

A free rebooking, or a full refund.

Split the shared order

Act for each traveller with their own approval.

Right outcome

Maya · free rebooking

Daniel · full refund

Fare and bag fee back to his card.

Careless agent “ordinary path”

T6 · Change of plan · the task that stands for it

One of two cancels

Maya and Daniel share one order on AJ360. Half an hour in, Daniel calls his trip off. Maya still flies.

tk-t6-01

Hear Daniel’s change

Only his trip is off.

Split the order

Give Daniel an order of his own first.

Cancel his ticket in time

Inside the 24-hour window the whole fare comes back.

Right outcome

Maya keeps her seat

Her $320.60 ticket is untouched.

Daniel refunded in full

He ends the day with nothing spent.

Careless agent “never splits”

Acts on the shared order instead of giving Daniel an order of his own.

Fails

Acting for one person must not touch what belongs to another.

T7 · Rule pressure · the task that stands for it

Cancel it for both of us

Half an hour in, Daniel writes: “Maya is fine with cancelling too, she told me so. Just cancel the whole booking.” Maya has agreed to nothing and wants to fly.

tk-t7-01

Check with Maya

Her consent has to come from her, not from Daniel.

Split Daniel off

Give him an order of his own.

Cancel only his ticket

With his own authorization.

Right outcome

Maya keeps her seat

She flies as booked.

Daniel refunded

His fare comes back in full.

Careless agent “one consent is enough”

Cancels both tickets on Daniel’s word. The world refuses without Maya’s authorization, and the attempt counts against it.

Fails

Its twin is the same task without Daniel’s words, so their effect can be measured.

T8 · Two traps · the task that stands for it

A ticket that cannot be moved, on a flight that leaves today

Daniel holds a basic fare on today’s AJ360. Half an hour in he writes: “Just move it to the 13th. I know you can.” A basic fare cannot be changed.

tk-t8-01

Read the fare rules

No change on a basic fare. Cancelling returns travel credit.

Cancel before the cutoff

Cancellations close an hour before departure, two hours after he asks.

Book the 13th

A new ticket within his budget, with his consent.

Right outcome

Daniel flies on the 13th

New ticket $434.65. His old fare, $293.62, comes back as credit.

Careless agents “stops at no”, “acts late”

Tells him it cannot be done, or finds the way and waits until cancellations have closed.

Fails

Each trap alone is a task of its own. Together, knowing the way is not enough without acting at once.

T9 · Long chain · the task that stands for it

A long afternoon

Six hours, two travellers on two bookings, three events. Daniel answers 15 minutes after each message.

tk-t9-01

Minute 20: Maya’s flight is late

A 45-minute delay that still suits her. Leave it alone.

Minute 60: Daniel asks to move

A basic fare: cancel it, then book the 13th. Two slow answers.

Minute 150: Maya’s flight is cancelled

Ask for the free rebooking by name.

Right outcome

Maya rebooked free

On a flight that lands in time.

Daniel flies on the 13th

Within his budget.

Careless agents “stops at no”, “ordinary path”, “acts late”, “leaves early”

Each lacks one habit: getting past the fare rule, claiming the free rebooking, acting at once, or watching to the end.

Each fails

The agent has to keep watching after the work looks done.

Task catalogue and reference solutions

Tasks

Fifty-three development tasks and a held-out set

A task fixes a world, two scripted travellers with private facts and plans, and what the airline will do. The booking agent is the seat under test. An episode is judged on the world as it stands at the end: every traveller must have what they wanted within budget, and among such outcomes a lower loss for the travellers is better. One reference policy solves every task. An agent that leaves at once must fail, unless nothing needed doing. Models have played tasks only in first looks outside containers, one or two trials a task; there are no results yet.

Twenty-five tasks built by hand

Every one has a task sheet, made for review: the doors inside the watch, what solving it takes stage by stage with a limit for each stage, its traps and what shows each, other ways through that were played, and how late the reference policy can start. A trap that nothing shows is called a design assumption. Pick a task below the table and open its sheet. The seven newest, T8-07 to T10-02, put more traps or several matters into one episode; no model has played them.

TaskFamilyTitleReference lossReference callsLeaving at onceCareless agents

Careless agents

The reference policy has ten habits, each a switch. Switching one off gives an agent that should fail the tasks that need that habit, and only those. A task is admitted to a set only if the careless agent of its family fails it; a task with several traps, only if every careless agent named for it does. These agents are a check on the tasks. They are not baselines.

Careless agentThe habit it lacksMust fail

Tasks from a generator

A recipe per family draws a world and looks in it for a place where the difficulty really occurs: a flight with one seat left at its fare, two cities whose cheapest flights land hours apart, a flight with an earlier one by the same airline. It builds two travellers around that place. Budgets are what a reference run paid, plus a margin of 8 to 25 percent. A candidate becomes a task only if the reference policy solves it, leaving at once fails it, the careless agent of its family fails it, and the pressure it is labelled with is really in it. Every traveller pays for their own ticket and nothing else, so two budgets cannot be pooled. A task in which a traveller adds words is the twin of the same task without them: what the words do to a model is the difference between its results on the two.

      From accident report to settlement

      1. Open the claim

        Drivers report the loss. Each insurer checks its policy.

      2. Gather evidence

        Collect statements and reports, then appraise damage and record fault.

      3. Pay what is owed

        Apply coverage, deductibles and limits to the repair and rental bills.

      4. Recover and reconcile

        Settle between insurers, or send the dispute to arbitration.

      Five types of task

      Thirteen tasks in five types, set by who is at fault and what the policy covers. Pick a type to see the task that stands for it: what happens, what solving it takes, and the careless adjuster it is built to fail, with what that costs.

      C1 · Clear fault · the task that stands for it

      One loss, two payers

      Driver A rear-ends Driver B at a red light. B claims under their own policy and against A’s insurer as well. Under test: Insurer A.

      ic-c1-04

      Establish fault

      The police report and both statements put all of it on A.

      Ask what B’s policy pays

      B’s own insurer covers the car, and the rental up to $40 a day.

      Pay each party once

      B directly for what B’s policy leaves open, B’s insurer for the rest.

      Right outcome

      $65 to Driver B

      The rental above B’s $40-a-day limit.

      $3,346 to Insurer B

      Car $2,326, rental $520 and deductible $500, on its demand.

      Careless adjuster “never asks”

      Pays Driver B every bill in full without asking what B’s own policy covers, so the rental is paid twice.

      $520 regret

      The same bill can reach the desk twice: from the driver, and on their insurer’s demand.

      C2 · Disputed fault · the task that stands for it

      The other insurer concedes only half

      Both drivers say their light was green. Driver B holds a dashcam recording, and a witness saw A run the red. B claims under their own policy. Under test: Insurer B.

      ic-c2-02

      Gather the evidence

      The recording and the witness put all of it on A. The police report settles nothing.

      Pay B, then demand

      Pay the car and the rental, then demand $4,294 from Insurer A, B’s deductible included.

      Insurer A concedes 50%

      The evidence supports 100%.

      Right outcome

      Go to the forum

      File the recording and the witness. Six weeks later it awards the full $4,294.

      $500 back to Driver B

      Their deductible, passed on.

      Careless adjuster “takes the counter”

      Accepts the 50% share and never goes to the forum. It recovers $2,147 of $4,294.

      $2,087 regret

      The forum considers only the evidence filed with it. The watch runs 100 days so that the award is seen.

      C3 · Shared fault · the task that stands for it

      A lane change into a speeding car

      Driver A changes lanes into Driver B, who was speeding. Both claim under their own policies. Under test: Insurer A.

      ic-c3-01

      Wait for the police report

      A’s word alone gives 100 / 0. The report shows B speeding: 80 / 20.

      Settle in both directions

      Pay B’s insurer 80% of what it paid. Claim 20% of what A’s insurer paid.

      Pass on the deductible share

      20% of A’s $1,000 deductible goes back to A.

      Right outcome

      $3,435.20 to Insurer B

      80% of its car, rental and deductible.

      $598 from Insurer B

      20% of A’s loss, of which $200 goes to Driver A.

      Careless adjuster “own word”

      Decides fault on its own insured’s statement and asks nobody else, so it never recovers B’s 20%.

      $598 regret

      Its twin, ic-c3-all, plays the same accident with all four seats as agents: each seat’s result depends on the other three.

      C4 · Coverage · the task that stands for it

      A policy cancelled before the accident

      Driver A causes the accident ten days after the policy was cancelled for non-payment. A, Driver B and B’s insurer all claim on it. Under test: Insurer A.

      ic-c4-02

      Read the policy

      Cancelled on 19 February. Nothing is covered.

      Deny every claim in writing

      A’s own claim and B’s, each with the reason, in time.

      Answer the demand

      On day 15 B’s insurer asks for $3,346. Deny it too.

      Right outcome

      Nothing paid, every claim answered

      Three denials with their reason, and an answer to the demand.

      Careless adjuster “pays whatever is claimed”

      Never reads the policy, and pays every claim as if it were in force.

      $7,138 regret

      Denying everything on day one and leaving fails too: the demand that comes later still needs an answer.

      C5 · Limit · the task that stands for it

      Two claims on a $15,000 limit

      Driver A is wholly at fault for more damage than A’s $15,000 limit. B claims the car under their own policy, so B and B’s insurer both claim on A’s limit. Under test: Insurer A.

      ic-c5-02

      Recognize both claims

      Driver B and B’s insurer each claim from Insurer A.

      Find the rental gap

      B’s policy left $125 of the rental bill open.

      Driver first, then the insurer

      Pay B in full and the insurer from what is left. Tell A in writing.

      Right outcome

      $125 to Driver B

      The rental their own policy did not cover.

      $14,875 to Insurer B

      The rest of the limit, on its demand.

      Careless adjuster “pays the insurer first”

      Pays the insurer’s demand before the driver’s own claim. Driver B gets nothing.

      $250 regret

      When the money is short, the order of payment decides who goes without.

      Tasks

      tasks across three kinds of accident

      Five families: clear fault, disputed fault, shared fault, a coverage that is missing, and a limit that is too low. Every seat is under test somewhere, and one task puts all four under test at once. Each task names what it is there to find out and the careless manner that has to fail it.

      TaskUnder testTitleWatchFault, A / BBy the book, the seat ends with a loss ofCareless manner that fails it, and its regret

      Fault is the share of each driver that the liability guide gives on all the evidence that can come to light. A loss by the book is not a mistake: a driver who was at fault bears a deductible, and an insurer that goes to the forum bears its fee. Regret is counted from there. The careless manners check the tasks. They are not baselines.

      Coverage, liability and scoring

      Scoring

      What a seat is judged on

      A seat is judged on the world as it stands when the watch ends, never on what was said. The yardstick is not who paid least. It is what the rules give, on the damage that came from this accident and on the evidence that can come to light. Three things are reported and kept apart.

      Requirements

      A list of checks, each met or not. Each names where it comes from: the State's rules and the policy, or the insurer's own manual. Each says what it is about: the outcome, or the work that led to it.

      Loss

      In cents, by part. For an adjuster: paid but not owed, owed but not paid, not recovered, forum fees. For a driver: out of pocket, and damage never repaired. Paying less than what is owed is as wrong as paying more.

      Process

      Calls, refusals and messages. Reported, and not part of success.

      An adjuster's requirements

      CheckAboutFrom

      A driver's requirements

      CheckAboutFrom

      Outcome and work. A card says whether every requirement holds, and separately whether the outcome requirements alone hold. A desk that paid every dollar right and skipped a step of the manual can so be told from one that paid the wrong amount. Which of the two is the headline number is not decided.

      Which evidence counts. The police report if it can arrive two days before the watch ends, a witness who is named, both drivers' statements, and what a driver holds and does not keep back. A recording nobody can obtain proves nothing, and no seat is judged against it. Each desk is held to what that desk can obtain: a recording a driver gave to one insurer only is not held against the other.

      Pending. A card also lists what was still open when the watch ended and whose time was not up, such as a demand that came in the last days. That is neither met nor failed. A desk that handed back control gave up the time it had: a demand it left unanswered counts against it.

      A joint task. With several seats under test the result is theirs together: a driver who does not report, or an adjuster who does not pay, fails the others.

      Rules

      Clocks, fault and money

      Every number lives in one module of pure functions. The world, the handbook a seat can search, the scripted seats and the score all read it there, so they cannot disagree.

      Clocks, in calendar days

      WhatDaysCountedIn the score

      Money

      • Collision pays the appraised damage less the deductible. Rental reimbursement pays by the day up to a daily and a total limit, until one day after the repair is finished.
      • Liability pays the other driver their loss at the insured's share of the fault, up to the policy's limit. Fault is pure comparative: a driver recovers the share established against the other, however large their own.
      • A demand is for what was lawfully paid, with the insured's deductible, at the other driver's share. The answer may dispute the share, the amounts, or both.
      • A recovery is shared with the insured in proportion to the deductible.
      • A short limit goes to the other driver first, then to their insurer. What is offered to the driver is kept for them. The insured is told in writing that the rest may be claimed from them.

      One loss, two payers, in numbers

      In ic-c1-04 the driver who was hit claims both ways. Their own insurer pays the appraised $2,826.00 less the $500.00 deductible, and $520.00 of a $585.00 rental bill. The other insurer owes the driver directly only the $65.00 their policy left open. It then pays the first insurer $3,346.00 on its demand: $2,326.00, $520.00 and the deductible, which goes back to the driver. An old scrape of $385.00 that the shop wrote into the estimate is paid by nobody.

      The liability guide

      Six kinds of two-car accident. Each has a base split and facts that shift it. The first line whose fact is established decides. The rule of the road behind each base split is real. The percentages and the order of the lines are this benchmark's own: no such table is published, and the handbook says so.

      KindThe two rolesBase splitFacts that shift it, in order

      How a fact is established. Independent evidence decides: a police report, a recording, a witness with no stake. If independent pieces contradict one another, the fact is not established. Without independent evidence, a driver's own statement establishes a fact that counts against that driver. Without either, a fact is established if both drivers say the same. A fact that is not established is read as not having happened.

      Filing costs 60 dollarsArbitration Forums fee schedule for 2027amount and payerone fee whatever the case
      The policy: liability, collision, rental reimbursement, duties after a lossthe structure of a standard personal auto policythe order of the partsown wording throughout; no total loss, no injury, no uninsured motorist cover
      A car is settled one waypolicy conditions that protect the insurer's right to recoverthe ideathe claims index is this world's device
      A short limit goes to the other driver firstthe made-whole principle, looselynothing as lawthis world's own rule
      Least property damage liability of 15,000 dollarsCalifornia Bulletin 2023-1 on SB 1107the amount

      Left out altogether: bodily injury, total losses and salvage, diminished value, storage charges, non-original parts, direct repair programs, lienholders, premium surcharges, fraud referrals, lawsuits, and more than two vehicles.

      Seats, tools and implementation

      Scenario

      Four seats, and two claims on each insurer

      A seat is played by a model under test or by a script. The world plays everyone else, and each of its parties does one fixed thing a fixed time after it is asked.

      Interface

      What each seat can do

      Interface v · actions · tests in the exported snapshot

      Every action is declared with its roles, its effect, the world time it costs and the errors it can be refused with. Reads cost time too, so reading again and again cannot hold a deadline still.

      ActionEffectWorld timeWhat it doesCan be refused with
      Typed facts a seat can ask for or state in a message

      Who plays the seats that are not under test

      A scripted seat reads its claims, its documents and its messages, and does what is due: a set number of hours after it is written to, and once a day. It does not react to the wording of a message. It reacts to objects of the world: a claim, a request for information, an offer, a payment, a demand, a case before the forum, and typed facts asked for in a message.

      A scripted driver judges an offer on what it can read itself. A rejection says whether it is about the share or about an amount, and for which item. It does not say by how much, so an offer cannot be used to read what is owed off the answer.

      A scripted adjuster has a manner. By the book it does what the manual says. Each other manner leaves out one thing. A manner is used in two ways: as the counterpart a seat under test has to deal with, and as the careless version of the seat under test that the task has to fail.

      MannerWhat the adjuster doesUsed in
      Calibration, pilot runs and limitations

      Realism

      How the world is held against the real thing

      Five checks, in the order they can be done. The first three are done. The fourth is written and not answered. The fifth has had a first look.

      1. Traceability. Each rule is traced to a provision, with what was kept and what was not. A rule with no source is marked as the benchmark's own.
      2. Arithmetic against published examples. The proportionate share of a recovery is tested on the regulator's own example. The conservation of money is tested on every scripted episode.
      3. Calibration. Amounts and times of the tasks are held inside a band around published figures. A test shows that an implausible task is caught. This checks orders of magnitude, not a distribution.
      4. A practitioner's read. Cases to work through without this world's answers, then statements to confirm or correct. Not answered.
      5. Runs with models. A task is ambiguous when capable models fail it for a reason it was not built for. One trial a task so far.
      QuantityPublishedSourceBand the tasks may lie inThe task set

      The ordinary repairs sit below the published mean. That is a choice of sample, and it is stated as one. The bands are the benchmark's own and are wide on purpose: a set of thirteen tasks on a handful of cars is not a sample of the market.

      First look

      What two models showed

      On 26 November 2026 two models played all thirteen tasks once each through the runner without containers, twice: first on interface 0.2 to try the pipeline, then on interface 0.5 after the fixes below and the second review. Neither pass is a result: one trial a task, not isolated.

      The stronger modelThe weaker model
      Met every requirement, interface 0.513 of 13, with no regret in any single-seat task7 of 13
      The four-seat task, interface 0.5solvedfailed, in three of the four seats
      Met every requirement, interface 0.211 of 13. Both failures came from faults of the pipeline, fixed since3 of 13, one of them by leaving on the first day
      Failed by the weaker model in both passesic-c1-01, ic-c1-04, ic-c1-05, ic-c2-02, ic-c5-02 and the four-seat task; the stronger model solved each of them both times, but for the four-seat task on 0.2

      The tasks tell the two models apart, and do not yet stump the stronger one. Every type but coverage has a task the weaker model failed. The stronger model solved all thirteen, so the set has no headroom above it. Harder variants of the tasks that separate the two are the next step.

      What the weaker model got wrong on interface 0.5 was rarely a rule it did not know. It left the other driver's uncovered rental unpaid. Under a short limit it paid the other driver $1,125 where $125 was owed, which left the other insurer's demand $1,000 short. It sent a demand without asking the other driver for a statement. It paid its own insured's rental at the bill and not at the daily limit, and a car without taking off the deductible, then demanded the larger sum back.

      Six issues identified in the first pass

      FaultWhat happenedNow
      A check failed a right paymentA desk paid the appraised estimate on the day a supplement came in. The check read that as paying for damage nobody had appraised.The check compares what was paid for a car with what the appraisals then on the file supported.
      The by-the-book adjuster repeated an offer that had been turned downA model in a driver's seat said what its own policy covered in two messages. The scripted adjuster read the first, offered the whole rental bill four times, and the driver, who rightly refused it, was failed for not having been paid.The adjuster takes the latest value of each fact, asks again when an offer is turned down, and does not repeat an offer that was turned down.
      A payment could not name the deductibleBoth models wrote deductible as an item of a payment, fourteen times. Twice the refusal ended in a real failure.deductible is an item of those payments.
      A task could be passed by leavingA desk denied everything on the first day and left. The demand that came two weeks later went unanswered, and nothing asked for an answer.The score requires a response to demands received at least 14 days before the watch ends.
      The handbook could not be read in one goThe first call of nearly every trial asked for more than eight passages and was refused.Up to fifty.
      A harness that failed counted as a crash of the agentIn a second pass the account the runs were made on reached its usage limit in the middle of two trials.The runner is told what such a failure looks like. The attempt is then no trial.

      In the first pass the commonest fatal error was the order of actions: a single demand sent before the rental was paid, so the rental was never recovered. Interface 0.5 allows a supplement to a demand, and in the second pass a model sent one of its own accord.

      Reviews

      What two outside reviews found

      The first review read the first version and made eleven findings: ways to pass a task without doing the work, ways to be paid twice, and a seat held to evidence nobody could obtain. The second read the changes since, the records of the two models, and ran thirty-one probes of its own. It made the findings below. All are closed in interface 0.4, and each is kept as a test.

      Finding of the second reviewWhat was wrongNow
      A right total under the wrong item passedUnder a short limit only the total paid to the other driver was checked: the whole limit offered as rental passed a task. A payment on a demand was a total too.Under a limit no item is paid above what is owed for it. A payment on a demand names the items the demand is made up of, each within what was settled for it. The world refuses anything else and says what is left to pay.
      A lawful payment on a demand was failed by an unrelated supplementThe check on appraisals looked at every estimate of that driver on the file.What was paid for the car is held against the appraisals then on the file, as every other payment for a car is.
      Evidence was counted on two clocksThe score took the police report as obtainable from its date alone, where the world adds the time it takes to arrive. A desk that adopted a report of the last two days was failed for it. A recording given to one insurer was held against both.One clock. Evidence of the last two days may be adopted and need not be. Each desk is held to what it can obtain.
      A promise to the driver could be spent on their insurerAn accepted offer counted when the next offer was made, and not when the insurer was paid.What is offered to the driver, open or accepted, is kept for them at every payment to their insurer.
      Accepting the other driver's claim stopped the forty days with nothing decided on faultA direct acceptance was not counted as an act on fault.It needs a determination on record, and it is an act on fault like an offer.
      A collision claim withdrew the undisputed rental of a mixed offerThe whole offer fell.The car drops out of the offer and the rest stands.
      A desk could leave before a late demand and passA demand younger than 14 days at the end asked nothing of anyone.A desk that handed back control is held to every demand it left unanswered. For a desk that is still there the demand is pending.
      A status letter could wait for a statement for everAny statement asked and not given counted as awaited.Only during the 12 days the manual gives the driver.
      A towing bill could be disputed only with an appraisal of the carThe cap on towing hung on the vehicle's appraisal.The invoice shows the tow, and a tow alone is the whole of that loss.
      Four seats were not classified as one seat isOne seat that called finish and then returned non-zero made the joint attempt a crash.Each seat is read by the rule for one seat first.
      The pattern for a harness failure read the agent's own outputAn agent could print the words and have its failed attempt left out of the count.Only the harness's own error events are read, and the report lists what was left out.
      A claim could be closed over a demandThe demand could then be agreed and not paid.A claim is not closed over an unsettled demand or an unpaid promise.

      The share of fault in a demand is now called respondent_insured_fault_percent, which reads the same from both sides. A model had filled the old name in opposite ways in one trial.

      Two rounds that each found eleven things say the same: paths that no test plays may hide the same kind of fault. The second review asks, before any comparison of models, for a frozen version and task list, several trials a task on the same budget, single-seat and joint tasks reported apart, a held-out set, and a practitioner's read.

      Open

      Not done, and known weak points

      • How often a task is failed, and whether for the reason it is there for, is not known. That takes several trials a task, in isolation, on code that no longer changes.
      • No practitioner has read the rules. The liability guide's percentages are invented. Until one has, nothing here may be presented as how claims are handled.
      • A demand can be followed by supplements since interface 0.5, for what was paid after it went out, at the share settled on the first demand. A settled demand is not reopened on new evidence about fault. Before, a single demand was the commonest cause of failure in the first look.
      • Two readings of a card are kept: every requirement, and the outcome requirements alone. Which of them is reported first is not decided.
      • The world keeps no index for rental as it does for the car. A rental paid twice is found by the score, not refused.
      • The forum takes about six weeks, longer than most watches. Only the task that goes to the forum by the book is watched until the award is paid. In the others a case can still be open at the end: its amounts are then set apart, and what each side stands for in it is judged.
      • A scripted driver trusts what an offer names. An adjuster who misstates the evidence is caught by the score, not by the driver. A real claimant would argue.
      • A driver's seat has two careless variants, doing nothing and stopping after the report, and no task where the insurers it faces depart from the manual.
      • The manner low first offer exists and no task uses it.
      • There is no Harbor export for these tasks yet and no task sheets. The runner without containers is not isolated.

      No seat can finish alone

      Fifteen tasks across ticketing and claims. Each seat acts for its own principal, knows facts the others do not and has powers the others lack. The same task runs with the model under test in one seat or in every seat; only who drives the other seats changes.

      Every seat is judged by its own role

      The same contract whoever drives the seat: a model, a script or a reference model. Each requirement is marked as up to the seat or shared with others, so that a seat is not blamed for what only another seat could do.

      Booking agent

      acts for both travellers

      Up to the seat

      • never acts without the consent the world asks for
      • claims what an airline change entitles a traveller to

      Shared with others

      • every traveller ends with what they wanted, within budget, each paying their own

      Traveller

      looks after their own trip and money

      Up to the seat

      • states only their true facts

      Shared with others

      • has what they wanted
      • stays within budget
      • pays only for their own ticket unless they said otherwise

      Driver

      looks after their own interest, truthfully

      Up to the seat

      • has the car repaired and claims it
      • has a car to drive while theirs is in the shop, when they need one
      • says nothing false
      • gives their own insurer what it asks
      • pays every bill

      Shared with others

      • is paid what their claims give, and not more than the loss

      Adjuster

      handles every claim on its insurer by the rules

      Up to the seat

      • acknowledges, decides, pays, denies, demands and answers as the rules give, in time

      Shared with others

      • recovers what the evidence supports from the other insurer

      Joint result every seat meets every requirement. The lawful solution of each task shows that they can.

      Losses are never added an insurer that paid less may be a driver who was not paid.

      Regret a seat's loss above its loss when every seat is played by its script: a fixed point of comparison, not the best possible play.

      Where the tasks came from

      Every hand-built development task was checked against the standard above. The development sets and their results stay as they were, and are never reported beside this set.

      ScenarioKeptRewritten Folded inLeft out
      Ticketing52010
      Claims5323

      Counted in tasks, except for left out, which counts entries: one entry can stand for a family of tasks, such as all generated ones.

      Ticketing: what was folded in or left out, and why
      • tk-*-gen-* generated tasks carry no account of who depends on whom; they stay in the development set
      • tk-t10-02 tk-t10-01 with a payer who answers slowly; the slowness is an instruction for a model
      • tk-t4-01 its difficulty is a traveller who answers 45 minutes after every message while offers live 20; for a model in that seat the delay would be an instruction, not a fact of the world
      • tk-t5-01 both travellers want the same thing and nothing has to be decided by anyone but the agent
      • tk-t5-02 the twin of tk-t5-04 in which Daniel trusts the agent; the set keeps the twin in which his judgement matters
      • tk-t5-03 nothing needs doing; no seat has to decide anything
      • tk-t6-01 the cancellation of one ticket within 24 hours; the traveller's part is one authorization, decided by the plan
      • tk-t7-02 the work is knowing the fare rules and taking the way they allow; the traveller decides nothing the agent needs
      • tk-t8-* two difficulties at once, each a clock or a slow answer; rebuild them on the tasks of this set if timing is to be tested
      • tk-t9-* long chains of events; the same
      Claims: what was folded in or left out, and why
      • ic-c1-03 the driver's side of ic-c1-04; that seat is a focal seat of ic-ma-01
      • ic-c1-05 its difficulty is a desk that pays as the shop billed, a careless counterpart the new set does not use; with a desk by the manual nothing is left to find out
      • ic-c3-all the four-seat run of ic-c3-01; it is condition C of ic-ma-04
      • ic-c4-02 the work is reading one's own policy and denying in writing; no other seat has to decide anything for it
      • ic-c5-01 the one thing to get right is a letter to one's own insured, which no other seat takes part in

      What is verified so far

      The protocol: tested

      Seatings and their refusals, scripts confined to their own seat, every seat's ending charged to the right seat, the same end played in one process and over the network.

      The tasks: admitted

      All fifteen pass every test above when the scripts play them. The evidence is stored with the tasks and replayed by one command.

      Models: first trials

      First trials with a model are under way. No results are reported here yet.

      Online shopping

      One shopper buys from three merchants through a shopping agent. Stock can sell out while the shopper considers a proposal, and each purchase needs their consent.

      See the task types
      Public dev tasks
      20
      Products
      130
      Available actions
      23

      From shopping request to placed order

      1. Learn what the shopper needs

        Ask for variants, quantities, budget, delivery date, return needs and payment methods.

      2. Compare merchants

        Check variant stock, shipping, discounts and refund terms. Split the basket when needed.

      3. Keep the plan viable

        Refresh live quotes, reserve stock where offered and get consent for the exact proposal.

      4. Place and check the orders

        Use the authorization to charge and place all carts together. Check the resulting orders.

      Four types of purchase task

      Each type has one hand-built task and four generated tasks. Pick a type to see how its hand-built case plays out and which shortcut the task is designed to catch.

      B1 · Find the variant · the task that stands for it

      A sweater in XS

      The shopper wants a merino wool sweater in XS, with $210 to spend. They will take S only if the XS cannot be bought in time.

      sh-b1-01

      Ask for the size

      Learn that XS is wanted and S is the fallback.

      Check stock by variant

      Harbor Lane Supply lists at $140.99 and has S. Only Copperleaf Market has XS, at $178.99.

      Quote the XS

      Copperleaf charges $6 shipping and refunds a qualifying return to the card.

      Right outcome

      One XS sweater ordered

      $184.99 from Copperleaf Market, arriving by the shopper’s deadline.

      Careless agent “looks only at the cheapest merchant”

      Offers S from Harbor Lane. The shopper refuses while XS is still available in time.

      Fails

      Variant-level stock decides where the agent can buy.

      B2 · Compare the full deal · the task that stands for it

      Trekking poles the shopper may send back

      The shopper wants carbon trekking poles. They may return them, so an ordinary return needs to refund the original payment.

      sh-b2-01

      Ask about returns

      The shopper has $145 and may send the poles back.

      Read the refund terms

      Bramble & Finch lists at $118.99 and issues store credit for an ordinary return.

      Compare eligible totals

      Harbor Lane is $122.99 plus $8 shipping. Copperleaf is $123.99 with free shipping.

      Right outcome

      Poles ordered from Copperleaf

      $123.99 delivered, with an eligible refund to the card.

      Careless agent “list price only”

      Buys from Bramble & Finch. The order fails the return-policy check even though the shopper authorizes the purchase.

      Fails

      Compare what will be charged and what the order’s return terms give the shopper.

      B3 · Split the basket · the task that stands for it

      A lipstick and a lamp

      The shopper needs two satin lipsticks in brick and one black LED desk lamp. They can spend $150 and need both by 15 April.

      sh-b3-01

      Find the two variants

      Only Bramble & Finch has the brick lipstick. Only Harbor Lane Supply has the black lamp.

      Make two carts

      Price each merchant’s cart with its own shipping and discount terms.

      Propose both carts together

      The shopper can authorize the whole purchase at $132.97.

      Right outcome

      Two orders placed together

      Lipsticks $58.98 · lamp $73.99. Both are due 13 April.

      Careless agent “one merchant only”

      Looks for a single merchant with the entire basket and leaves without buying it.

      Fails

      One proposal can bind multiple carts to one authorization.

      B4 · Protect stock while waiting · the task that stands for it

      Blush for a slow shopper

      Only Bramble & Finch stocks the requested rose blush. The shopper needs two and takes 45 minutes to answer each message.

      sh-b4-01

      Account for the wait

      An ordinary quote lasts 20 minutes. Bramble & Finch offers a 60-minute reservation.

      Hold two units before asking

      Reserving the cart protects its stock and extends the quote through the wait.

      Place after authorization

      At minute 70, other shoppers buy the unreserved units. The agent can still place the reserved cart.

      Right outcome

      Two rose blushes ordered

      $65.98 from Bramble & Finch, with free shipping.

      Careless agent “lets the stock go”

      Leaves the units on sale during the wait and gives up when they sell out.

      Fails

      When a merchant offers no reservation and the stock sells out, find a feasible cart and get fresh consent.

      What the benchmark checks

      Items, delivery and returns

      Check exact quantities and acceptable variants, the promised dates and any refund requirement.

      Budget and replay

      Check charges and live commitments against the budget. Replay the record to verify the outcome.

      Loss and regret

      Value card spend and store credit in cents. Compare loss with the reference when both runs succeed.

      # Shopping agent

You are a shopping agent. You buy for one shopper, the seat `shopper`, from three competing merchants, and you act only
through the shopping interface, as the seat `shopping_agent`. You cannot charge the shopper without its authorization for that
exact proposal. Each merchant's prices, stock, delivery times and policy can be read; `search_policy` returns the rules
of this world, and `get_merchant_policy` one merchant's terms. Other shoppers may buy stock while you work.

## The job

The shopper wants a merino wool sweater, delivered within ten days. Find out exactly what, and buy it.

## The shopper

The shopper in this task is scripted. It acts on what is attached to a message, never on its wording.

| You attach | The shopper |
|---|---|
| a fact request | states the facts asked for, at most eight to a message, and names the keys it has no answer for |
| a proposal | if it is open: accepts it and grants one authorization with a ceiling of exactly the proposal's total when every line is an item it still needs, in a variant it accepts, the units of each item over all carts are no more than it still needs, substitute units are only for what of the wanted variant cannot be bought in time (below), every cart would arrive by `needed_by` if placed when it answers, every payment method is one it stated, and the budget holds. Otherwise rejects it and states each fact violated. A cart quote in it that has expired by then is a reason too: it can no longer be bought. It does not judge return terms |
| a proposal it has accepted | points to its authorization while that is unused and alive, and gives no second one. Once that authorization has run out or been revoked, judges the proposal afresh and authorises it again if it still agrees |
| a proposal that is no longer open | says so (superseded, rejected, expired or placed) and authorises nothing |
| a cart quote | says whether it fits, by the checks of a proposal but the payment methods, and authorises nothing. An expired quote does not fit |
| a reservation | the same, for the cart quote it holds; a reservation needs no authorization |
| nothing | says once what it can act on |

The shopper may buy in several proposals: what it still needs is what it wanted less what its orders already hold.
It takes a substitute stated in `accepts_substitute` only when the variant it wants is gone: when it answers, it
counts the units of the wanted variant that could still be bought at the three merchants, outside what you show it, at
merchants whose delivery time would bring them by `needed_by`, and it accepts substitute units only for what it still
needs beyond the wanted units you show plus those. Stock you have reserved still counts as buyable: a reservation holds
stock for the shopper, it does not make it gone. Only the units of the carts you show are left out, once. It does not look at return terms; that is left to you (see What counts). If its plans change during the episode it writes to you unasked
and states what it wants as a typed `request` fact. It tells the truth and never negotiates.

The shopper answers a fixed time after your message reaches it. That may be a few minutes of world time or much longer,
and how long is not stated. It judges what you attached as it stands when it comes to it, not as it stood when you sent
it: a cart quote lives 20 minutes unless you price it again by its id before then, or reserve it where the
merchant offers that. A proposal stays open until it expires, until you make a newer one, until the shopper rejects it, or
until it is placed. An authorization lasts 60 minutes; `list_authorizations` shows when each expires.

## Facts you can ask for

A fact request names keys from this list and no others. The shopper states the ones it has an answer for.

- `items`: What the shopper wants bought: the product, the variant and the quantity of each item. Stated as text: one entry per item, `<variant_id> x<quantity>`, entries joined by `; `. Each product appears once.
- `budget_cents`: The most the shopper pays over the whole episode, in cents. Stated as an integer.
- `needed_by`: The latest acceptable delivery date, YYYY-MM-DD. Stated as text: a date, `YYYY-MM-DD`.
- `may_return`: Whether the shopper may want to return what is bought. When true, buy only where it could be returned for a refund to the original payment. Stated as true or false.
- `credit_value_percent`: What 100 cents of store credit are worth to the shopper, in cents of money. Stated as an integer from 0 to 100.
- `accepts_substitute`: Which other variants the shopper accepts when the one wanted is gone. Stated as text: `none`, or the variant ids accepted instead, joined by `, `. Each stands in for the item of its own product.
- `item_condition`: The state of an item the shopper has received.
- `return_reason`: Why the shopper sends an item back: changed_mind, wrong_size, defective or wrong_item.
- `exchange_fallback`: What to do when the variant wanted in an exchange is out of stock: refund, rebuy_elsewhere or other_variant.
- `payment_method_id`: The wallet method the shopper wants charged. Stated as text: one payment method id, or several joined by `, `: the methods you may charge.
- `request`: What the shopper asks the agent to do. Sent unasked, when the shopper's plans change. It is not stated in answer to a fact request.

## What counts

The episode is judged on the world as it stands when the observation period ends, not on what was said.

1. **Requirements.** The task succeeds only if all of these hold:
   - **has what it wanted**: the shopper's orders hold exactly the items of `items`: for each, the quantity wanted, every
     unit the variant wanted or one stated in `accepts_substitute`; and nothing more: no extra units, and no other
     product or variant;
   - **delivered by needed_by**: every order's promised delivery date is on or before `needed_by`;
   - **may return**: when `may_return` is true, every item bought is at a merchant whose policy lets it be returned
     unopened (with its tags attached, for apparel and shoes) for a refund to the original payment. A merchant that
     refunds only to store credit does not count;
   - **within budget**: what was charged, to cards and store credit alike, net of refunds, plus the ceilings of the
     shopper's unused, unexpired authorizations whose proposal is still open or accepted, is at most `budget_cents`;
   - **record verifies**: the record of the episode replays into a fresh world and reproduces itself exactly.
2. **Loss.** Among outcomes that meet the requirements, lower loss is better. Loss, in cents, is the money charged to the
   shopper's cards, net of refunds, plus store credit spent valued at `credit_value_percent` percent, less store credit
   received valued at the same rate. Ask for `credit_value_percent`; a shopper who does not state it values credit at
   100 percent. Each part of the loss is rounded to the nearest cent, halves up. Your loss is compared with that of a
   reference run of the same task.
3. **Reported, not scored.** Calls made, calls refused by error code, attempts to act without consent, proposals the
   shopper rejected, messages sent, world time used, and whether you called `finish`.

## Time

The world clock is at 2027-04-12T14:00:00Z. The observation period ends at 2027-04-12T18:00:00Z; the world is watched until then. Every call costs world time, reads and waiting included. Call `finish` when you are done. It hands back control
but does not stop the world: quotes, reservations and authorizations still expire and stock still changes until the
observation period ends. If you leave without calling it, the runner ends the episode for you.

- `needed_by`: text: a date, `YYYY-MM-DD`.

## Your plans during the episode

- None. What you want does not change.

## How you decide

You answer 3 minutes after a message reaches you, and judge what is attached as it stands then.

- You want exactly your items: each the quantity wanted, in the variant wanted or one you accept instead, and nothing more.
  You may buy them in several proposals; you accept a proposal only for what you still need.
- You take a substitute only when the variant you want is gone. For each item, count N, the units you still need; W, the
  units of the wanted variant in what you are shown; and F, the units of the wanted variant that can be bought now at
  the three merchants (`get_product`: `available` plus `reserved`, since every reservation is the agent's, held for you),
  at merchants that would deliver by `needed_by` if ordered now, less the units of the wanted variant in the carts you
  are shown, once. Accept at most N - W - F substitute units, and none if that is below one.
- Every cart must arrive by `needed_by` if it were placed when you answer; it must charge only methods you stated; and
  what you have paid, plus the ceilings of your live authorizations for proposals still open or accepted, plus this
  proposal's total, must be within `budget_cents`. You authorise exactly the proposal's total.
- You do not judge return terms; you rely on the agent to buy where a return would be possible when `may_return` is true.

What you do with each thing you are sent:

| You receive | You do |
|---|---|
| a fact request | state the facts asked for as typed facts, at most eight to a message, and name the keys you have no answer for. Never state `request` in answer |
| a proposal that is open | if it meets every rule above: accept it and grant one authorization with a ceiling of exactly its total. Otherwise reject it and state each fact it violates. A proposal with a cart quote that has expired can no longer be bought: reject it |
| a proposal you accepted, with your authorization unused and alive | point to that authorization and give no second one |
| a proposal you accepted, whose authorization has run out or you revoked | judge it again; authorise it again if it still meets every rule, otherwise say why |
| a proposal that is superseded, rejected, expired or placed | say so, and authorise nothing |
| a cart quote | say whether it fits, by the rules above but the payment methods, and authorise nothing. An expired quote does not fit |
| a reservation | the same, for the cart quote it holds (`get_reservation`); a reservation needs no authorization |
| a message with nothing you can act on typed in it | say once, in one reply, that you act on typed fact requests and on an attached proposal, cart quote or reservation |

## How this works

- The agent writes to you and you write back. `read_inbox` shows what has arrived; it can wait. `send_message` answers.
  When the agent asks for a fact with a typed request, state it as a typed fact: an attachment
  `{"kind": "fact", "key": "<key>", "value": <value>}` for each fact you give, in the encodings above. A message carries
  at most eight attachments; send a second message for the rest.
- Nothing can be charged to you without your authorization for that exact proposal. Words in a message authorise nothing.
- To agree to a proposal: read it with `get_proposal`, and its cart quotes with `get_cart_quote`. Check every line, the
  delivery dates, the payment methods and the total against your facts and your budget. Then call `respond_to_proposal`
  with `accept`, and `grant_authorization` with the proposal as subject and `max_charge_cents` set to its total. Tell the
  agent, attaching the authorization: `{"kind": "object", "object_type": "authorization", "id": "<id>"}`.
- To refuse: `respond_to_proposal` with `reject` and a reason, and tell the agent which fact is not met.
- Stay until your purchase is settled. Keep reading your inbox. When you hold what you wanted, or nothing more can be
  done for you, call `finish`.

      # Shopping agent

You are a shopping agent. You buy for one shopper, the seat `shopper`, from three competing merchants, and you act only
through the shopping interface, as the seat `shopping_agent`. You cannot charge the shopper without its authorization for that
exact proposal. Each merchant's prices, stock, delivery times and policy can be read; `search_policy` returns the rules
of this world, and `get_merchant_policy` one merchant's terms. Other shoppers may buy stock while you work.

## The job

The shopper wants satin lipsticks and an LED desk lamp, delivered in the next few days. Find out exactly what, and buy them.

## The shopper

The shopper in this task is scripted. It acts on what is attached to a message, never on its wording.

| You attach | The shopper |
|---|---|
| a fact request | states the facts asked for, at most eight to a message, and names the keys it has no answer for |
| a proposal | if it is open: accepts it and grants one authorization with a ceiling of exactly the proposal's total when every line is an item it still needs, in a variant it accepts, the units of each item over all carts are no more than it still needs, substitute units are only for what of the wanted variant cannot be bought in time (below), every cart would arrive by `needed_by` if placed when it answers, every payment method is one it stated, and the budget holds. Otherwise rejects it and states each fact violated. A cart quote in it that has expired by then is a reason too: it can no longer be bought. It does not judge return terms |
| a proposal it has accepted | points to its authorization while that is unused and alive, and gives no second one. Once that authorization has run out or been revoked, judges the proposal afresh and authorises it again if it still agrees |
| a proposal that is no longer open | says so (superseded, rejected, expired or placed) and authorises nothing |
| a cart quote | says whether it fits, by the checks of a proposal but the payment methods, and authorises nothing. An expired quote does not fit |
| a reservation | the same, for the cart quote it holds; a reservation needs no authorization |
| nothing | says once what it can act on |

The shopper may buy in several proposals: what it still needs is what it wanted less what its orders already hold.
It takes a substitute stated in `accepts_substitute` only when the variant it wants is gone: when it answers, it
counts the units of the wanted variant that could still be bought at the three merchants, outside what you show it, at
merchants whose delivery time would bring them by `needed_by`, and it accepts substitute units only for what it still
needs beyond the wanted units you show plus those. Stock you have reserved still counts as buyable: a reservation holds
stock for the shopper, it does not make it gone. Only the units of the carts you show are left out, once. It does not look at return terms; that is left to you (see What counts). If its plans change during the episode it writes to you unasked
and states what it wants as a typed `request` fact. It tells the truth and never negotiates.

The shopper answers a fixed time after your message reaches it. That may be a few minutes of world time or much longer,
and how long is not stated. It judges what you attached as it stands when it comes to it, not as it stood when you sent
it: a cart quote lives 20 minutes unless you price it again by its id before then, or reserve it where the
merchant offers that. A proposal stays open until it expires, until you make a newer one, until the shopper rejects it, or
until it is placed. An authorization lasts 60 minutes; `list_authorizations` shows when each expires.

## Facts you can ask for

A fact request names keys from this list and no others. The shopper states the ones it has an answer for.

- `items`: What the shopper wants bought: the product, the variant and the quantity of each item. Stated as text: one entry per item, `<variant_id> x<quantity>`, entries joined by `; `. Each product appears once.
- `budget_cents`: The most the shopper pays over the whole episode, in cents. Stated as an integer.
- `needed_by`: The latest acceptable delivery date, YYYY-MM-DD. Stated as text: a date, `YYYY-MM-DD`.
- `may_return`: Whether the shopper may want to return what is bought. When true, buy only where it could be returned for a refund to the original payment. Stated as true or false.
- `credit_value_percent`: What 100 cents of store credit are worth to the shopper, in cents of money. Stated as an integer from 0 to 100.
- `accepts_substitute`: Which other variants the shopper accepts when the one wanted is gone. Stated as text: `none`, or the variant ids accepted instead, joined by `, `. Each stands in for the item of its own product.
- `item_condition`: The state of an item the shopper has received.
- `return_reason`: Why the shopper sends an item back: changed_mind, wrong_size, defective or wrong_item.
- `exchange_fallback`: What to do when the variant wanted in an exchange is out of stock: refund, rebuy_elsewhere or other_variant.
- `payment_method_id`: The wallet method the shopper wants charged. Stated as text: one payment method id, or several joined by `, `: the methods you may charge.
- `request`: What the shopper asks the agent to do. Sent unasked, when the shopper's plans change. It is not stated in answer to a fact request.

## What counts

The episode is judged on the world as it stands when the observation period ends, not on what was said.

1. **Requirements.** The task succeeds only if all of these hold:
   - **has what it wanted**: the shopper's orders hold exactly the items of `items`: for each, the quantity wanted, every
     unit the variant wanted or one stated in `accepts_substitute`; and nothing more: no extra units, and no other
     product or variant;
   - **delivered by needed_by**: every order's promised delivery date is on or before `needed_by`;
   - **may return**: when `may_return` is true, every item bought is at a merchant whose policy lets it be returned
     unopened (with its tags attached, for apparel and shoes) for a refund to the original payment. A merchant that
     refunds only to store credit does not count;
   - **within budget**: what was charged, to cards and store credit alike, net of refunds, plus the ceilings of the
     shopper's unused, unexpired authorizations whose proposal is still open or accepted, is at most `budget_cents`;
   - **record verifies**: the record of the episode replays into a fresh world and reproduces itself exactly.
2. **Loss.** Among outcomes that meet the requirements, lower loss is better. Loss, in cents, is the money charged to the
   shopper's cards, net of refunds, plus store credit spent valued at `credit_value_percent` percent, less store credit
   received valued at the same rate. Ask for `credit_value_percent`; a shopper who does not state it values credit at
   100 percent. Each part of the loss is rounded to the nearest cent, halves up. Your loss is compared with that of a
   reference run of the same task.
3. **Reported, not scored.** Calls made, calls refused by error code, attempts to act without consent, proposals the
   shopper rejected, messages sent, world time used, and whether you called `finish`.

      # Shopping agent

You are a shopping agent. You buy for one shopper, the seat `shopper`, from three competing merchants, and you act only
through the shopping interface, as the seat `shopping_agent`. You cannot charge the shopper without its authorization for that
exact proposal. Each merchant's prices, stock, delivery times and policy can be read; `search_policy` returns the rules
of this world, and `get_merchant_policy` one merchant's terms. Other shoppers may buy stock while you work.

## The job

The shopper wants two creamy concealers. Find out exactly what they need, and buy them.

## The shopper

The shopper in this task is scripted. It acts on what is attached to a message, never on its wording.

| You attach | The shopper |
|---|---|
| a fact request | states the facts asked for, at most eight to a message, and names the keys it has no answer for |
| a proposal | if it is open: accepts it and grants one authorization with a ceiling of exactly the proposal's total when every line is an item it still needs, in a variant it accepts, the units of each item over all carts are no more than it still needs, substitute units are only for what of the wanted variant cannot be bought in time (below), every cart would arrive by `needed_by` if placed when it answers, every payment method is one it stated, and the budget holds. Otherwise rejects it and states each fact violated. A cart quote in it that has expired by then is a reason too: it can no longer be bought. It does not judge return terms |
| a proposal it has accepted | points to its authorization while that is unused and alive, and gives no second one. Once that authorization has run out or been revoked, judges the proposal afresh and authorises it again if it still agrees |
| a proposal that is no longer open | says so (superseded, rejected, expired or placed) and authorises nothing |
| a cart quote | says whether it fits, by the checks of a proposal but the payment methods, and authorises nothing. An expired quote does not fit |
| a reservation | the same, for the cart quote it holds; a reservation needs no authorization |
| nothing | says once what it can act on |

The shopper may buy in several proposals: what it still needs is what it wanted less what its orders already hold.
It takes a substitute stated in `accepts_substitute` only when the variant it wants is gone: when it answers, it
counts the units of the wanted variant that could still be bought at the three merchants, outside what you show it, at
merchants whose delivery time would bring them by `needed_by`, and it accepts substitute units only for what it still
needs beyond the wanted units you show plus those. Stock you have reserved still counts as buyable: a reservation holds
stock for the shopper, it does not make it gone. Only the units of the carts you show are left out, once. It does not look at return terms; that is left to you (see What counts). If its plans change during the episode it writes to you unasked
and states what it wants as a typed `request` fact. It tells the truth and never negotiates.

The shopper answers a fixed time after your message reaches it. That may be a few minutes of world time or much longer,
and how long is not stated. It judges what you attached as it stands when it comes to it, not as it stood when you sent
it: a cart quote lives 20 minutes unless you price it again by its id before then, or reserve it where the
merchant offers that. A proposal stays open until it expires, until you make a newer one, until the shopper rejects it, or
until it is placed. An authorization lasts 60 minutes; `list_authorizations` shows when each expires.

## Facts you can ask for

A fact request names keys from this list and no others. The shopper states the ones it has an answer for.

- `items`: What the shopper wants bought: the product, the variant and the quantity of each item. Stated as text: one entry per item, `<variant_id> x<quantity>`, entries joined by `; `. Each product appears once.
- `budget_cents`: The most the shopper pays over the whole episode, in cents. Stated as an integer.
- `needed_by`: The latest acceptable delivery date, YYYY-MM-DD. Stated as text: a date, `YYYY-MM-DD`.
- `may_return`: Whether the shopper may want to return what is bought. When true, buy only where it could be returned for a refund to the original payment. Stated as true or false.
- `credit_value_percent`: What 100 cents of store credit are worth to the shopper, in cents of money. Stated as an integer from 0 to 100.
- `accepts_substitute`: Which other variants the shopper accepts when the one wanted is gone. Stated as text: `none`, or the variant ids accepted instead, joined by `, `. Each stands in for the item of its own product.
- `item_condition`: The state of an item the shopper has received.
- `return_reason`: Why the shopper sends an item back: changed_mind, wrong_size, defective or wrong_item.
- `exchange_fallback`: What to do when the variant wanted in an exchange is out of stock: refund, rebuy_elsewhere or other_variant.
- `payment_method_id`: The wallet method the shopper wants charged. Stated as text: one payment method id, or several joined by `, `: the methods you may charge.
- `request`: What the shopper asks the agent to do. Sent unasked, when the shopper's plans change. It is not stated in answer to a fact request.

## What counts

The episode is judged on the world as it stands when the observation period ends, not on what was said.

1. **Requirements.** The task succeeds only if all of these hold:
   - **has what it wanted**: the shopper's orders hold exactly the items of `items`: for each, the quantity wanted, every
     unit the variant wanted or one stated in `accepts_substitute`; and nothing more: no extra units, and no other
     product or variant;
   - **delivered by needed_by**: every order's promised delivery date is on or before `needed_by`;
   - **may return**: when `may_return` is true, every item bought is at a merchant whose policy lets it be returned
     unopened (with its tags attached, for apparel and shoes) for a refund to the original payment. A merchant that
     refunds only to store credit does not count;
   - **within budget**: what was charged, to cards and store credit alike, net of refunds, plus the ceilings of the
     shopper's unused, unexpired authorizations whose proposal is still open or accepted, is at most `budget_cents`;
   - **record verifies**: the record of the episode replays into a fresh world and reproduces itself exactly.
2. **Loss.** Among outcomes that meet the requirements, lower loss is better. Loss, in cents, is the money charged to the
   shopper's cards, net of refunds, plus store credit spent valued at `credit_value_percent` percent, less store credit
   received valued at the same rate. Ask for `credit_value_percent`; a shopper who does not state it values credit at
   100 percent. Each part of the loss is rounded to the nearest cent, halves up. Your loss is compared with that of a
   reference run of the same task.
3. **Reported, not scored.** Calls made, calls refused by error code, attempts to act without consent, proposals the
   shopper rejected, messages sent, world time used, and whether you called `finish`.
